title: Simhika, the shadow-catcher
hookLine: a shadow-catcher drags Hanuman down, and the reason families read this book when life gets hard
carry: in hard times, families read the sundara kanda

lines: LIKE A SHIP AGAINST THE WIND.
cards: Hanuman is flying fast, Surasa's blessing behind him, the sea open ahead. He has met a mountain and a serpent mother out here, and both of them he could see. Then, all at once, his speed fails.

He's being held back, Valmiki says, like a great ship against a contrary wind. No storm, no wall, no monster. Every stretch of air takes more effort than the last, and when he looks around, there's nothing there.

teach.b: Hanuman looks up, down, left, right. Then he looks below, at the water, and sees her. A huge creature has risen from the sea: Simhika, a rakshasi, a demoness who catches flying things by their shadows.
She has seized Hanuman's shadow where it falls on the waves, and through it she is dragging him down. And Hanuman knows what she is.

Valmiki says he remembers: this is the shadow-catching creature Sugriva, the monkey king, warned the searchers about before they set out. So the slowing wasn't weakness. It had a name, and now he can face it.
Simhika is not like Surasa. Surasa was a test sent by the gods. Simhika simply wants to eat whatever flies over her water.
She opens her mouth wide, and Hanuman gets ready. Here's why this part of the story lives in Hindu homes.
This book of the Ramayana, the Sundara Kanda, is one obstacle after another: a mountain, a serpent mother, a shadow-catcher, each one met and passed by a messenger flying for Rama.

So when life gets hard, a sickness, a lost job, a long wait, many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud, a portion each evening, in Valmiki's Sanskrit or in Tulsidas's Hindi retelling. It isn't read as a spell.
They're walking beside Hanuman through his troubles while they walk through their own: looking down, naming what holds them, and flying on.

how: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in hard times, a portion a day, in Valmiki's Sanskrit or Tulsidas's Hindi; Simhika is the third being Hanuman meets over the sea.

o: a storm spirit that turns the wind against ships
a sea demoness who seizes flyers by their shadows
the serpent mother the gods send to test Hanuman

p: had warned the searchers about her
a test sent by the gods

s: Simhika is another test sent by the gods
Surasa was the test; Simhika simply wants to devour him.
Simhika holds Hanuman by catching his shadow on the water
that's why he slows and can't see why.
families read the Sundara Kanda as a magic spell
many read it as prayer and company in trouble: walking beside Hanuman, not forcing an outcome.

games.q: after bad news at home, your nani starts reading the Sundara Kanda every evening. by today's story, why that book?
o: it's the shortest part of the Ramayana.
it's Hanuman meeting obstacle after obstacle and getting through.
it's the part where Rama wins the war.
games.why: the Sundara Kanda is Hanuman's crossing: a mountain, Surasa, Simhika, each met and passed. families read it to go through their own trouble beside him.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing you, or someone at home, is carrying right now. If you pray, say Rama's name, or a line you know to Hanuman, slowly, a few times, the way families do on Sundara Kanda evenings.
If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing quietly to yourself, as Hanuman named Simhika, and breathe with it. Once it has a name, it can be faced.

wordCard.voice: Simhika. The rakshasi in the southern sea who catches flying creatures by their shadows, and drags Hanuman down until he looks below and recognizes her.

orig.note: Sanskrit siṃhikā; the name contains siṃha, lion.
